title: Handling and restraining rabbits safely
subtitle: A rabbit held incorrectly can break its own spine trying to escape. The grip matters.
excerpt: Rabbits have powerful back legs and a skeleton not designed to bear twisting forces. A rabbit that panics in your arms and kicks hard enough to straighten against a grip can fracture a lumbar vertebra. This tutorial covers the correct carry hold, table restraint for examination, and how to pick up a rabbit that does not want to be caught.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council handling guidance. RSPCA rabbit welfare notes. Judith Bell, Rabbits (Crowood Animal Series, 2012), chapter on handling. University of Wisconsin Extension small animal restraint notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A break in the lower spine of a rabbit, most commonly caused by the animal kicking powerfully while held incorrectly. Often fatal or permanently disabling.

Holding a rabbit by the loose skin at the back of the neck. Not a safe primary hold for rabbits — unlike cats, the skin stretches uncomfortably and the animal can still kick. Reserve for veterinary procedures only.

content.text: The back end of a rabbit is the dangerous end, not for biting, but for kicking. A hindquarter left unsupported during a pick-up can drive the animal into a rotation that snaps the lower spine. A
lumbar fracture
in a rabbit is not a recoverable injury. The correct grip prevents the hindquarters from swinging free.
The carry hold
There are two positions that work safely.

The first is the tucked hold: one hand cups the hindquarters firmly from beneath, the other hand supports the chest. The rabbit sits against your body with its head tucked against your forearm. This position keeps the spine straight and the back legs pointing away from you, not toward you, so a kick goes outward rather than into you.

The second is the football carry: tuck the rabbit facing backward under your arm, its rear against your hip, the hand on that side cupping the hindquarters, your other hand free. Useful when opening a hutch door single-handed.
Do not hold by the ears. Rabbits are not cats or dogs, the ears carry blood vessels and are a primary thermoregulation organ.
Do not allow the hindquarters to dangle unsupported at any point during the lift.
Do not use
scruffing
as a primary hold. It provides little control and stresses the animal.
Table restraint for examination
For ear checks, nail trimming, or checking the underside, a table with a non-slip mat is better than arms. The rabbit can feel all four feet on a solid surface and is calmer for it.
Set the rabbit down facing away from you on the mat. Keep one hand lightly across the shoulders.

For a rear examination, slide one hand under the belly and tip the rabbit gently onto its back in your lap or against a rolled towel. A rabbit on its back is typically still for 30-60 seconds, this is tonic immobility, a prey-animal fright response, not contentment. Keep the examination brief.

For an uncooperative animal, wrap it in a towel with only the head free, tucking the legs against the body. This is the safest method for nail trimming with two people: one holds the towel bundle, one trims.
Catching a rabbit that won't come to you

Chasing a rabbit around a hutch or run damages trust and increases stress for both of you. Instead, remove hiding spots if possible, then corner quietly. Walk toward the rabbit slowly and crouch as you get close, a crouching predator looks less threatening than a standing one.

Offer a treat from your hand first. Once the rabbit takes a step toward you, use the cup-from-beneath motion before it can reverse. Speed matters here but not force, a quick, confident scoop is less frightening than a hesitant grab.

attrs.cue: Rabbit scratches arms badly during carry
attrs.cause: Hindquarters not supported — the claws are the only anchor point available
attrs.fix: Firm up the rear-end support immediately. Wearing a long-sleeved thick shirt helps while you build technique.

attrs.cause: Hold loosened during carry or door was opened without both hands in position
attrs.fix: Do not attempt to catch the falling rabbit. Let it land. Rabbits dropped from below hip height on a soft surface are usually uninjured. Check immediately for limping or abnormal posture.

attrs.cue: Rabbit goes limp immediately on being picked up
attrs.cause: Fear-induced tonic immobility — a normal prey response, not safe unconsciousness
attrs.fix: Complete your task quickly. Set the rabbit down and move away to let it recover. A rabbit held in tonic immobility for too long can die of stress-induced heart failure in rare cases.
